source: AD-S37#Q&A on writing process and 'Red Bottoms'
finding: ADÉLA tells Vogue CS that 'Red Bottoms' started when she looked at a worn-out shoe and recognised her own state in it. The title names a luxury object (red-soled heels), but the idea behind it was a frayed one, so the brand works as a stand-in for her own run-down state rather than as a flex. One student reviewer (AD-S45 para 4) singled out 'Red Bottoms' as the best showcase of her writing, and another (AD-S46 para 6) read it as asking whether she would still be loved with her flaws.
why_it_matters: A status object seen in a worn or broken state can carry a confession while the title still reads as glamour.
when_not: If the listener never gets the worn-out side of the object, the title reads only as brand-dropping.

source: AD-S37#Q&A on process, creative blocks and collaborators
finding: ADÉLA describes a two-stage process: ideas start when she has time alone to reflect, but she prefers to finish them in scheduled co-writes where she talks through ideas, melodies and memories with collaborators. She says the team writes a lot of songs and many bad ones, and that this is the only way to reach the good ones. On flat days she keeps writing and uses the frustration itself as material; one PRIMA track is essentially that frustration on a loop. She names Blake Slatkin as her closest studio collaborator and says she has written a lot with Julia Michaels and Billy Walsh.
why_it_matters: In a session, telling memories out loud is part of the writing, not a warm-up before it, and a session that produces bad songs is the expected route to a good one.
when_not: She describes no method for choosing which of the many songs survive, so this tells you nothing about editing.

source: AD-S16#quote block 6 (before 'Starving Artist' heading); AD-S42#'What Has ADÉLA Said' para 2
finding: In Capital's Making The Album write-up, ADÉLA says a session set up to write an upbeat song went wrong because she wasn't in an upbeat mood. The talk drifted to sex toys, producer 'Blake' (presumably Slatkin) mentioned a Hitachi, and they first wrote a deliberately bad upbeat song before turning to a sad one about intimacy fading in a relationship. The page puts its song headings after the quotes, so which track the anecdote belongs to is ambiguous; the Hitachi detail points to 'Hitachi'. Separately, via Teen Vogue as quoted by Just Jared, she says 'Hitachi' opens on a stack of harmonies.
quote: We were trying to write an upbeat song
why_it_matters: An off-topic joke in the room can become the title, and the song can then go the opposite way from the joke (sad, not cheeky), which gives the title an edge.
when_not: The Arts Desk (AD-S35 para 4) warned that a novelty title like this risks gimmickry and survives only if the song fully commits to its premise.

source: AD-S17#quoted paras 1-3; AD-S10#para 10; AD-S15#'The Event' paras 1-2
finding: ADÉLA says that while writing the album she watched Eyes Wide Shut and wanted more Nicole Kidman in it. At a Golden Globes party she felt she had no business attending, dressed up in a tight corset, she thought that she felt like Nicole Kidman. She sums the song up as being about feeling like Nicole, so the celebrity's name is a shorthand for a feeling, not a song about the actress. Sources disagree on the order of events (Capital puts the film the day before the party, Songfacts after) and on who first printed the quote (W Magazine or Rolling Stone).
quote: I feel like Nicole and that's what the song is about.
why_it_matters: A celebrity-name title works when the name stands for one specific feeling the narrator borrows (here, poised movie-star glamour), not when the song is about the celebrity.
when_not: NME (AD-S26 para 9) called it one of the album's few misses even as it became a UK top-5 single (AD-S50), so critics and listeners split on it.

source: AD-S20#exchange on Slovak background and family; AD-S37#Q&A on Slovak directness
finding: On NPR, ADÉLA calls herself a very blunt person, links that to a feistiness she sees in Eastern European women, and names her mother as the bluntest person she knows. She calls herself dry and sarcastic and says humour makes it easier to face things that aren't funny. In Vogue CS she contrasts Slovaks, who say it straight away, with Americans, who circle around the point. Taken together she presents bluntness as cultural and the joke as a way to carry hard material.
why_it_matters: A narrator who states the uncomfortable thing straight away, then undercuts it with dry humour, can get hard material across without sounding heavy.
when_not: Rolling Stone (AD-S24 paras 5, 8) found the stated, told-not-shown moments the weakest, so bluntness about feelings works less well than bluntness about facts.

finding: ADÉLA says 'Therapy' was recorded around Grammy week with her voice almost gone, with heavy Auto-Tune as a result. The first take ran about 15 minutes of her talking over the beat, and it was cut down to a three-minute track. She calls it more of a therapy session than a song; its subjects are frustration with executives, missing her younger sister and moving away. The song was edited down from a stream of consciousness rather than built from a sectioned draft.
quote: That was just rambling on the beat.
why_it_matters: Recording a long unfiltered ramble over the beat, then cutting it down, is one way to find the lines a sectioned draft would never produce.
when_not: Several reviewers found the result the album's weakest: lyrics 'especially simple' (AD-S47 para 10), hard to endure vocally (AD-S45 para 19), a slog (AD-S44 para 4), and the lowest user track score on AOTY (AD-S28). Diary material needs a strong edit.

finding: ADÉLA tells Vogue CS that 'KGB' was meant literally and partly as a joke, and that listeners who expected a metaphor were confused; she added an on-screen disclaimer in the video saying she supports Ukraine. W Magazine describes the song's persona as a fly on the wall absorbing American pop culture like a spy, with a lyric about learning English as a child. Learning English is therefore subject matter in the song. No fetched source has her discussing what it is like to write lyrics in her second language.
why_it_matters: A loaded political noun used as a comic, literal persona can be misread as a metaphor or a political statement, so the frame may need to be made explicit, as she did in the video.
when_not: Rolling Stone (AD-S24 para 5) felt 'KGB' tried too hard to convince, while Arts Desk (AD-S35 para 2) called it over the top but tightly written; the comic persona splits critics.

source: AD-S18#paras 7-10; AD-S12#para 2; AD-S37#Q&A on 'Ain't in LA'
finding: ADÉLA gives three linked sources for 'Ain't In LA'. The first is a photo of her mother at 18 in front of Western pop posters that her grandfather smuggled in from Germany. The second is Lorde's 'Royals' and 'Team', which meant a lot to her as a child and which she wanted to echo by writing about being outside the zeitgeist. The third is frustration, as someone who lives in LA, at the same people and beauty standards being praised. In Vogue CS she says LA in the title works as a metaphor, because she was tired of celebrity-focused songs.
quote: Where it's like being not in the zeitgeist, right?
why_it_matters: A place name can stand for a whole value system, and the song can define itself by refusing that place rather than describing it.
when_not: Some Singles Jukebox critics (AD-S36) heard the 'Royals' model as derivative, and St. Asaph found the outsider stance patronising.

source: AD-S13#subject matter and Theron Thomas sections; AD-S10#para 9; AD-S9#para 5
finding: Songfacts describes verse one as a run of small domestic details (a shared bedroom with a younger brother, hand-me-down clothes, Madonna and Destiny's Child posters), with verse two widening from one girl to girls in unknown cities everywhere. The title and chorus are built on a negation (where the cool ones are not). A pitched-down, distorted male refrain or intro is performed by Theron Thomas (W para 9; Songfacts calls it chopped and screwed and notes it recalls 'We Can't Stop', which he co-wrote). The FADER heard the effect as a nod to early A$AP Rocky and Bangerz-era Miley. Credited writers: Jergová, Walsh, Thomas, Slatkin, Brady (AD-S13, AD-S4).
why_it_matters: Moving from one specific girl in verse one to a crowd in verse two turns a personal memory into an anthem, and a second voice on the refrain can carry the song's period reference.
when_not: Whether Thomas wrote the refrain or only performs it is not established, and nothing about the chopped-and-screwed sound is verifiable here without audio.

source: AD-S36#blurbs: Kuppermann, Doyle, St. Asaph, Leah Isobel, Mathers, Varela, Alatorre
finding: Seventeen Singles Jukebox critics averaged 5.76/10 and split sharply. Kuppermann (4) said the lyrics are too vague because the only named place is Los Angeles; Doyle (5) wanted specific Bratislava detail and called it tasteful to the point of blandness; St. Asaph (3) found a line about smaller towns patronising. Mathers (10) called the chorus great, Varela (8) praised the shout-along hook, and Leah Isobel (6) heard the chorus's negation as leaving an unsettling gap. Reviewer view: the hook carries the song, while the abstraction that lets every listener in is also what costs it specificity.
quote: Everything here is one step too vague.
why_it_matters: If a song is about the places outside the famous city, naming at least one of them stops the outsider stance from feeling generic.
when_not: For a chart anthem the vagueness may be deliberate: it became her first Hot 100 entry and a UK No. 12 (AD-S49, AD-S50), so the critics' preference is not the audience's.

source: AD-S48#entry #4 'Boys'; AD-S46#para 5; AD-S16#quote block 4; AD-S4#track notes
finding: Reviewers describe 'Boys' as built around spoken exchanges between ADÉLA and KATSEYE's Lara Raj that break up the verses and choruses; Wikipedia lists her as uncredited. RatingsGameMusic says the lyric compares male attention to a vending machine, and Pipe Dream (AD-S47 para 8) reads the song as wanting yet resenting male attention. In the Capital write-up ADÉLA says the lyric is about men who hover around her and her friends on nights out without engaging, and that she brought Raj in because their conversations are very funny. That quote sits under the 'Red Bottoms' heading; that it belongs to 'Boys' is my inference.
why_it_matters: Dropping real friend-to-friend banter into the gaps between sections can deliver attitude and comedy that a sung line would make too earnest.
when_not: The Arts Desk (AD-S35 para 3) found 'Boys' too minimal to convey the carelessness it aimed for.

finding: Critics disagree on whether her voice works best with or without a wink. Rolling Stone's Larisha Paul says she sings with steady eye contact rather than a wink, that she convinces most when showing rather than telling, and that the predictable moments ('KGB' trying too hard, plodding 'Marijuana' lyrics, 'Starving Artist' near a Tate McRae throwaway) fall flat. NME's Bailey Slater says the opposite: she shines brightest when winking at pop's cheekier side, and 'KGB' is pastiche-laden. In her own words she pairs vulnerability with swagger (AD-S3 para 3) and calls her stage choreography campy, knowing and almost ironic (AD-S10 para 7), though that remark is about dance, not lyrics.
quote: Predictable doesn't really work for her
why_it_matters: Decide line by line whether the narrator is winking or deadpan; critics punished the moments that were neither and simply stated the obvious.
when_not: Critics' readings of tone do not show what the writers intended.

source: AD-S44#para 4; AD-S45#paras 11, 19, 21; AD-S47#paras 10, 12; AD-S35#paras 3, 5; AD-S23#para 4; AD-S26#para 9
finding: The recurring criticism is aimed at the slower, sincere songs. A Sputnik user reviewer (low weight) says she has not yet learned to write convincingly sincere lyrics and calls 'Hitachi' and 'Therapy' a slog; The Post says the album wears its influences too openly; The Arts Desk says 'Marijuana' repeats ideas from other tracks and that parts of the album are simple homage; Pipe Dream reports fans finding the album tamer and more on-the-nose than her provocative EP. Other critics disagree: Clash calls 'Hitachi' terrific and NME says 'Hitachi' and 'Therapy' capture the turmoil of first heartbreak. Metacritic's aggregate is mixed-to-favourable (AD-S27).
why_it_matters: An artist whose edge comes from cheek needs her sincere songs to keep a specific, unexpected image; plain diary statements are where critics lost interest.
when_not: Two credible outlets found the ballads the emotional peak, so this is a split verdict, not a consensus.

finding: ADÉLA tells Clash she used to avoid writing about love and that PRIMA pushed her into love songs, which she now treats as an important human experience. She says she wanted the album to cover love, family, sex and insecurity about sex, and to be witty, young and girly but also smart and deep. Clash also paraphrases advice from Slatkin and Brady that writing to what people want produces the worst art; this is the interviewer's paraphrase, not the producers' words. In the label press release she says she mixed the hard with the soft and the vulnerable with the swagger.
quote: I had an aversion to writing about love
why_it_matters: Pairing opposite registers on purpose (witty with deep, swagger with vulnerability) gives an album its range, and the topic a writer has avoided can be where the new material is.
when_not: No producer or co-writer statement was found to corroborate how the sessions actually ran.

source: AD-F1; AD-F3; AD-F4; AD-F7; AD-S35#para 4; AD-S50
finding: My inference: at least five of the eleven PRIMA titles are loaded proper nouns or brand-type names ('KGB', 'Nicole Kidman', 'Red Bottoms', 'Hitachi', 'Marijuana'). In every case where she explains the origin, the noun stands for an emotional state, not the topic: a corset moment means feeling like a movie star, a worn shoe means being run down, a session joke becomes a song about fading intimacy, a spy agency stands for an immigrant kid soaking up American culture. The noun gets attention and provokes, while the song underneath does something else. It worked commercially for 'Nicole Kidman' (UK No. 4) but drew 'gimmick risk' and 'miss' verdicts from critics.
why_it_matters: When pitching a proper-noun title in a session, check what feeling the noun stands for; if nobody can say, it is only a novelty.
when_not: No source has her or a co-writer describing this as a deliberate method; it is a pattern I see across her accounts.

source: AA-S2#early-to-middle (chorus-chords passage; 'had the lyric before I knew' passage; second-verse passage)
finding: Carpenter says she already had the repeated title phrase before she knew what the song would be about. The phrase came out of a situation she was living through that week. The session's starting point was Antonoff's chorus chords: he played, watched what made her light up (and noticed when she pulled a face), and the phrase was matched to those chords. Carpenter also says she and Amy Allen wrote the second verse in about five minutes while Antonoff was changing the key, with Antonoff moving between instruments as the two of them worked on the words.
why_it_matters: A title phrase that a writer is already carrying around can wait for the right chord bed. The person playing can steer by watching the singer react, without arguing for an idea.
when_not: This is one session in which the artist brought her own phrase; it says nothing about rooms where no one arrives with a phrase.

source: AA-S2#~0.02, ~0.20, ~0.76, ~0.87 and the bridge passage (~two-thirds through)
finding: Carpenter says the subject (swinging between confidence and embarrassment over a man) was picked because she could frame it as funny. She describes needing to laugh while talking about something you could cry about, and calls the result 'desperately comical'. Antonoff says the best artists know when to be funny because it makes the next sad line sadder. In the bridge, which was missing at the end of the first day and finished about a month later at his LA studio, a sincere, heartbreaking line is followed straight away by a line that undercuts it with a joke. Antonoff calls that pairing the genius of her writing.
quote: all my favorite artists know exactly when to be funny
why_it_matters: Put the sincere line first and the joke right after it, so the laugh follows the hurt and makes it stronger instead of covering it.
when_not: My own inference, not from a source: if every line is a joke there is no sincere line for the humour to sharpen.

source: AA-S2#~0.50-0.60 (conversation and acting passages; melody-ending passage)
finding: Antonoff says many of the lyrics on these songs are literal things Carpenter said in conversation, and Carpenter agrees the song is really a conversation with herself. She says she treats singing as acting and pictures talking to the person as she sings, which lets her move between sung and spoken phrasing. She says she likes a line that is sung sweetly and then turns blunt two seconds later, and credits the give-it-to-them-straight women she grew up with, including her mother. She also says one melody ending was moved from high to low so the delivery would land. That is a text-only report; I have not heard the audio.
why_it_matters: Write down what the artist actually says in the room word for word, because the lyric may already be in it, and sing it as if speaking to someone rather than as a statement.
when_not: Speech copied straight into a lyric still has to fit the melody's stresses; Carpenter's note about moving a melody ending lower shows the delivery being adjusted to suit the words.

finding: Allen says that in sessions a flag often goes up that a line or note is too weird, too pop, too personal, or too specific and niche. She says that flagged part is usually the best part of the song, that people love it nine times out of ten, and that she tries to chase those moments. Her example is a profane word in Please Please Please that the writers laughed at, which became one of the most-loved parts of the song.
quote: usually the best part of the song
why_it_matters: The line the room is nervous about is a candidate to keep and test, not one to cut automatically.
when_not: Critics quoted on Wikipedia about Man's Best Friend (AA-S21: Slant, the Guardian, the Independent) said the profanity and innuendo were overused, so chasing the nervous line can tip into sameness.

finding: Allen says that when writing with artists she always starts with the chorus, which she calls the crux of the song. If someone later wants to redo the chorus, her instinct is that they should probably write a new song. For her own 2024 album she deliberately dropped chorus-first and wrote straight through from the first word to the last, as she did when she was younger, to break pop-song rules she had absorbed.
why_it_matters: In a co-write, settle the chorus first because everything else hangs off it. Writing from the top down is a deliberate alternative when the aim is a personal song rather than a hit.
when_not: Her own album shows she drops chorus-first when she is writing for herself.

finding: Allen says it was not really a disagreement, but a couple of weeks after the session McRae said she thought the chorus lyric was wrong. They then edited the song heavily and, in Allen's words, completely changed its concept. Allen says she trusts the artist because the artist has to sing the song for years and knows her own voice best. The only documented before-and-after facts are that the chorus lyric and the concept changed. Wikipedia (AA-S24) separately reports McRae saying a chorus line was reworded and that the song was rewritten and recorded in January 2023; no wording is available to me.
why_it_matters: When the artist rejects the chorus after the session, expect the concept to change rather than a word or two, and give the artist's ear for her own voice the final say.
when_not: This applies when writing for an artist; for a writer's own record there is no artist to defer to.

finding: Allen says she is notoriously bad at writing from a title someone hands her or from a planned idea; a title out of thin air feels like a puzzle to solve. She prefers to talk with the artist about what is going on in their life and stumble on the song from there. She also says she has spent the last couple of years trying to undo structural habits, for example when someone says a song should go straight to the chorus, because a song does not need every trick every time.
quote: it feels like I'm trying to do a Sudoku puzzle
why_it_matters: For this writer the title comes out of talking with the artist, not from a list of titles, and a missing section is sometimes the better choice.
when_not: Other writers do work from title lists; this is her stated preference, not a general rule.

source: AA-S5#Q&A answer to 'Some of the lyrics on Man's Best Friend are hilarious'
finding: Allen describes the Man's Best Friend sessions with Carpenter as swinging from vulnerable conversation to hysterical laughter within a minute. She says the two of them would look at each other and ask whether they were really going to say a line, then decide that they were. On Manchild, she credits Carpenter's self-awareness for a song that is melodic and beautiful but full of witty remarks that poke fun at herself. She does not describe how Manchild was written.
quote: Oh my God, are we going to say that?!
why_it_matters: Treat the moment both writers hesitate over a line as a decision to make out loud, and keep the line if both agree.
when_not: See AA-F4 for the critics' counterpoint about overuse.

finding: Allen says she did not know humour was something she could express in her writing until she met Carpenter. She says Carpenter was the first artist to invite her into her highs and lows while staying witty, and she places this in a line running back to Dolly Parton and John Prine. She says Adore You taught her that a song does not have to be serious and heart-wrenching. She also says she was taught that too many chords or too-personal lyrics lose listeners, and she cites the key changes on Carpenter's last two albums as proof that this is wrong.
quote: the listener is way more than capable of following you
why_it_matters: Humour and harmonic surprise are allowed in a hit, and listeners will follow an unexpected turn.

source: AA-S8#Q 'How did you and your co-writers write this song?' and Q 'How did this song come together?'
finding: Allen says Back to You started the night before the session, when she reconnected with a friend and thought about that relationship. The next morning she sang the co-writers (Micah Premnath and Trackside) a melody and an idea, and they wrote the song quickly. On Halsey's Without Me she says the writers were not trying to write an empowerment song; it became one. She notes that songs written as empowerment songs can come out cheesy or preachy.
quote: I sang them a melody and an idea I had.
why_it_matters: A melody plus the seed of an idea, both carried in from the writer's own life, can be enough to start a fast session. A theme like empowerment comes out better as a result than as the goal.
when_not: This is one documented melody-first case; no source I fetched has Allen calling herself generally melody-first or lyric-first.

source: AA-S9#Q&A 'Most of your songs are pretty dark' and 'Why do indie rock artists make such good pop songwriters'
finding: Allen says she usually reaches for harder emotions first and writes from something she is dealing with at the time. With artists, she listens for a subject they keep coming back to and writes from that. She writes with a guitar in hand, aiming for songs that could stand up on stage, and says you could strip the production off her co-writes and hear an indie rock song.
quote: I instantly go to something I'm dealing with right now
why_it_matters: Listen for the subject the artist keeps returning to in conversation and test whether the song works on one guitar before production.
when_not: She calls Adore You her first feel-good song, so the dark-first habit has exceptions.

finding: In this AP story, the account of how Espresso was written comes from co-writer and producer Julian Bunetta, not from Allen. He says the four writers (Carpenter, Allen, Steph Jones, Bunetta) were like kids having fun, laughing and playing, and links that energy to the song's cheerful sound and its nonsensical lines. Separately, Carpenter (AA-S16, NME relaying Apple Music and Vogue) says comparing an infatuation to a caffeine habit was fun to write and that the song captures a moment of unusual confidence. Allen gives no account of writing it in any source I could open.
quote: were kids having fun and laughing and playing
why_it_matters: A playful room can produce a hook that does not quite make sense on paper; the playfulness of the session is what produces it.
when_not: Nonsense needs confident delivery and a clear central image (here caffeine as infatuation); otherwise it reads as filler.

finding: Press coverage relayed on Wikipedia treats the chorus phrase as grammatically odd. Them discussed with a grammar writer whether it parses as one noun phrase or two side by side, and a linguist consulted by Vulture suggested it is not grammatical. Yet Vulture called the hook an instant earworm and the lyrics whimsical, and the phrase became a meme. The feature is a coffee noun used where an adjective or noun phrase would normally go, so the phrase holds attention because it does not quite parse. I could not open the original Vulture and Them pieces, so this is second-hand.
why_it_matters: A hook can work because it is slightly broken grammar delivered with total confidence, which makes listeners repeat it and argue about it.
when_not: My own inference: it works where the persona is confident and playful; in a sincere ballad the same oddness would read as a mistake.

finding: Press relayed on Wikipedia describes the song's language as insults delivered over sweet, upbeat melodies (People), as 'withering couplets' (Pitchfork), and as Carpenter comically laying into an ex (Variety). The page also notes a sarcastic tone in the intro. Billboard reports Carpenter's own description of the man in four blunt insulting adjectives. Allen (AA-F8) adds that the song also makes fun of the narrator herself. Together these describe a sweet melody carrying contempt, softened by the narrator mocking herself too.
quote: withering couplets
why_it_matters: Sarcasm goes down more easily when the tune is sweet and the narrator turns some of the mockery on herself.
when_not: Wikipedia gives no source for the 'sarcastic intro' description, and I did not open the Pitchfork, People or Variety reviews directly.

finding: No source I fetched describes Please Please Please as a plea that turns into a threat. Wikipedia's summary of the NYT, LA Times and Guardian reading is a famous woman's anxiety that her partner will embarrass her. My inference: the repeated polite title (a plea) combined with Carpenter's stated liking for being sung sweetly and then blunt two seconds later (AA-S2) is what lets the request carry a warning. The politeness is in the title, and the edge comes from what she asks him not to do. This reading is mine and not attributed to any writer.
why_it_matters: A polite repeated request can carry a warning if the verses spell out the consequence instead of the chorus.
when_not: Do not present this as the writers' intent; nobody in the fetched sources says it.

finding: Charlie Handsome (credited as Ryan Vojtesak) says 'Last Night' started as an eight-bar riff he had recorded as a phone voice note and chopped into a loop; one day in the studio the team pulled it up and wrote the song to it. He says his aim is to make beats that already sound like hits, so the room only has to find the right song to put on them. He also concedes, while saying writers shouldn't rely on it, that a hit-level hook lets weak verses get through. Separately, Ashley Gorley told Variety (CW-S3) that 'Last Night' and 'You Proof' were driven by the riff and feel Handsome created.
quote: you can get by with bad verses
why_it_matters: When a session starts from a loop that already sounds finished, the hook gets tested first and the verses are the most likely weak point, so check the verses on their own.
when_not: Starting from the loop suits short, groove-led songs; a story song whose payoff sits in the verses shouldn't start this way.

source: CW-S47#At a Glance form line; structural notes
finding: Hit Songs Deconstructed's public summary gives the form as I-B-A-B-VB-A-B-VB-O, running 2:39. A chorus comes before the first verse, and there is no pre-chorus but there is a post-chorus. Where a bridge would usually go, there is an unusual second chorus stanza, labelled a D section. This comes from a published structural analysis, not from listening; the site's melody and lyric breakdowns are paywalled and were not read.
quote: having its first chorus precede the first verse
why_it_matters: When the hook is the whole proposition, opening on the chorus and varying the chorus instead of writing a bridge keeps a short song on-message.
when_not: If the song needs a late change of perspective, such as a confession or a reveal, cutting the bridge removes the natural place to put it.

finding: Holler (CW-S46) and American Songwriter (CW-S45) both describe the song as a blunt argument fuelled by drink the night before. Afterwards the partner has walked out, and the narrator, who can't remember all of it, insists that night wasn't their last. Holler notes the title works two ways: as yesterday evening, and as the final night together. American Songwriter stresses that nothing is resolved; the fight is never settled and the narrator gets no answer.
why_it_matters: A title that is ordinary time language but can also mean 'the end' lets each chorus ask the song's question again without new words.
when_not: The double reading only survives while the verses keep the outcome open; once the fight is resolved, the second meaning goes dead.

song: I Had Some Help — Post Malone & Morgan Wallen
finding: Chandler Walters recalls a night at a Nashville bar when Post Malone bought shots for the whole room. Walters said he didn't know how they would get through it, and Charlie Handsome answered that they'd need some help. The article reports that this remark, future tense and plural, became the past-tense, first-person title, which reads as an admission; the next day was set aside to write a Morgan song for Post. Walters says his steel-guitar part became the sung verse melody, and ERNEST (CW-S7) puts the whole write at about 24 minutes, with Wallen and Post singing the demo that evening.
quote: Well, we're going to need some help
why_it_matters: Offhand room talk can become a title once its tense or person is shifted so that it confesses something.
when_not: The speed came from a pre-built track and a fixed artist target, so a 24-minute write is no model for a song still searching for its subject.

source: CW-S17#paras on the title track, 'Lies Lies Lies' and 'I Had Some Help'
finding: My inference across the sample is that Wallen's songs repeatedly take an everyday phrase whose second reading moves the blame. 'I Had Some Help' splits fault for a breakup (TODAY, CW-S9, says both narrators want their exes to take more responsibility). NPR's Ann Powers hears the title track 'I'm the Problem' starting as a confession and turning to accuse the ex (also Country Now, CW-S16), and 'Lies Lies Lies' moving from an attack on a lover to implicating the singer; Paste (CW-S19) singles out 'Kick Myself' for a double meaning on its title phrase. These readings are critics' and mine; no writer in the sources says they set out to make blame shift.
quote: quickly directs itself vindictively at an ex
why_it_matters: Ask where the blame points in the first chorus and whether the last chorus can point it somewhere else; that shift can be the song.
when_not: Repeated across a 37-track album, the move becomes the formula critics complain of (CW-F14), and a song that simply takes the blame may land harder.

source: CW-S21#Q&A 'Does the melody come easier to you than the lyrics?'; Q&A on 'Runnin' Outta Moonlight'
song: Runnin' Outta Moonlight — artist not verified
finding: In 2014 Gorley said he can produce a hundred melodies in the time it takes a room to find one idea worth writing about. In his account the scarce thing is the concept: words people want to hear that are easy to sing but put a twist on something familiar. His example of singability is a title: co-writer Kelley Lovelace brought a version along the lines of 'Wasting moonlight', and they settled on 'Runnin' Outta Moonlight' because it sang better. In 2023 (Variety, CW-S3) he added that he works out loud rather than on a notepad, and that the simpler a song sounds, the longer it can take to get it that simple.
quote: easy to sing but have a different twist on something
why_it_matters: Sing candidate titles out loud and pick the one that moves in the mouth, even if that means swapping a near-synonym.
when_not: Gorley gives no phonetic reason beyond 'sang better', so any vowel or rhythm explanation for the swap is speculation, not his method.

source: CW-S25#passages on the Copperman demo, 'It was just syllables', and 'American Kids'
finding: Shane McAnally (2015) describes a Ross Copperman demo on which Copperman sang vowel sounds that would make no sense written down, and recalls a line that began as nothing but syllables before words were fitted to it. In the same interview, apparently about 'American Kids', he says the room deliberately avoided a linear story and made every line an image. His test for a line is that he is still reacting to it two seconds after it has gone by. In this room, then, the sound and stress of a melody can be settled before the words exist.
quote: He's singing vowel sounds
why_it_matters: Before replacing a placeholder with a 'better' word, check that the new word keeps the vowel the melody was built on (my inference; McAnally states no such rule).
when_not: Fitting words to sounds can produce lines that sing well and say little; Steve Leslie's 2018 American Songwriter column (CW-S60) links loop-driven stress patterns to a loss of conversational writing.

source: CW-S27#'When It Rains It Pours' passage
song: When It Rains It Pours — Luke Combs
finding: Ray Fulcher says Luke Combs brought the title, and co-writer Jordan Walker, tired of writing another sad song, proposed reversing the idiom's usual meaning: a breakup sets off a run of good luck and in the end turns out to be a blessing. The Love Junkies describe a related move on 'Girl Crush' (CW-S28). Lori McKenna took the phrase from social media, where it usually means admiring another woman, and the trio used it for romantic jealousy; Hillary Lindsey says it could as easily have been an empowerment song, and that they never debated the title before writing.
quote: totally flipped it on its head
why_it_matters: Take an idiom with a fixed emotional charge and ask what the song becomes if that charge is reversed; the listener's expectation then becomes part of the hook.
when_not: If the reversal is the only idea and the verses add nothing to it, the song tends to read as a novelty (my inference).

song: Sangria — Blake Shelton (artist per article context)
finding: Josh Osborne says he held the title 'Sangria' for months because it seemed like a woman's drink, and it didn't fit a session with Sara Evans. It opened up when he asked how a man could sing it believably: she is the one drinking it and he tastes it when he kisses her, a single physical detail that makes the title true for that singer. Co-writer Trevor Rosen then pushed for odd phrasing in the chorus. Gorley gives a parallel case (CW-S23): the bridge of 'You're Gonna Miss This' came from a repairman's offhand remark about his grown children's ages, and Gorley stresses that it really happened.
quote: how would a guy sing a song called "Sangria."
why_it_matters: If a title doesn't fit the singer, look for a sensory detail that puts the singer in physical contact with it before you change the title.
when_not: A detail only reveals something if it changes who the narrator is or what they want; a run of props such as a tailgate or a mason jar is just decoration.

source: CW-S29#paras on title joke, talking-country influence, and Billboard quote
song: you look like you love me — Ella Langley & Riley Green
finding: Langley says the title came from a joke when Aaron Raitiere asked about her love life: a man who looks like he loves her is her cue to leave. She modelled the verses on the spoken 'talking country' she grew up with, and Riley Green wrote his reply verse later. Wikipedia (CW-S30) credits Langley, Green and Raitiere and describes two spoken verses, hers then his, before they sing the final chorus together. Langley doubted the song would be recorded because she was talking, not singing (CW-S31), refused her label's request to sing the verses (CW-S32), and Green says he thought the spoken verses were too traditional for radio.
quote: I thought the talking verses were probably too traditional
why_it_matters: Spoken verses under a sung chorus give a duet built-in turn-taking, and the first time the two voices sing together becomes the payoff.
when_not: This depends on a conversational, joke-driven premise; a solemn lyric spoken over a groove can sound like recitation.

finding: In a 2013 Boston Globe piece on the bro-country backlash, Shane McAnally agreed that formulaic was the right word for the trend: the same material rearranged, which he says everyone, himself included, writes. As a listener he wants to be surprised, and he will only reluctantly put someone in a truck, if the idea feels true and that is the only way to tell the story. In the same piece Zac Brown says he is sick of tailgate-in-the-moonlight songs, while Dallas Davidson defends the tailgate as a place where real life happens. Lainey Wilson's 'Heart Like a Truck' (CW-S51) shows the exception: after she judged a rockier first draft not honest, the truck was rewritten into a metaphor for a battered, durable self.
quote: It's a rearranging of the same thing
why_it_matters: Let a stock genre image in only if the story can't be told without it or if it becomes the song's metaphor rather than a prop.
when_not: This is one writer's personal standard; it is not evidence that listeners reject the images.

source: CW-S20#Q&A on co-writer numbers, difficult sessions, royalties, advice
finding: Gorley, credited on 'Last Night', 'I Had Some Help' and 'Love Somebody', criticises parts of the system he works in (Music Business Worldwide, 2022). He finds large co-writing teams strange, saying too many people can spoil a song; says royalty pressure makes writers think about radio too much and turn out songs that don't come from their soul, and says he will abandon a song that is only a 'B'. His advice to new writers is not to write a sequel to an artist's last release. In 2017 (CW-S22) he denied working from a formula, yet said the title 'Dirt On My Boots' wasn't special, since boots songs already existed, and that its value lay in how the whole song came together.
quote: don't write Part Two of whatever they just put out
why_it_matters: If a new idea mainly resembles the artist's last hit, it's a 'Part Two'; look for what is new in the angle or the execution.
when_not: Reusing a familiar word, like 'boots', is not reusing a concept, and Gorley's catalogue shows familiar titles can still succeed when the execution is new.

finding: Chartmetric's analysis of about 20,000 country songs found average credited writers per song rose from 1.8 in 2000 to 2.9 in 2022. Over the same period lyric repetitiveness, defined as 1 minus unique words over total words after common words are removed, rose from about 53% to over 61%. At the song level, more writers went with more repetition (p<0.0001), but total word count explained more of it, and the study shows correlation, not cause. Credit counts are a weak proxy for who was in the room: Saving Country Music (CW-S18) counts 52 writers on 'I'm the Problem', yet 'Love Somebody' lists six writers in Big Loud's release (CW-S10) and eleven on Wikipedia (CW-S11). Wikipedia also notes an interpolation of 'Tokyo Nights' (marked citation needed), whose artists include Shaun Frank, one of the extra names, so the interpolation is a plausible source of the extra credits.
quote: an observed rise in repetitiveness as the number of songwriters increases
why_it_matters: If a lyric's count of distinct words falls as more people work on it, check whether the repetition is a deliberate hook or what was left after compromise.
when_not: Repetition is part of how hooks work, so a high score is not a flaw in itself, and a credit list can include interpolated or production writers who never touched the lyric.

source: CW-S19#paras on recurring imagery and 'Kick Myself'
finding: Paste's 2025 review of 'I'm the Problem' says recurring images of whiskey, small-town drives and exes make the songs feel formulaic, with familiarity coming from repetition rather than vulnerability; it singles out 'Kick Myself' and the double meaning in its title as an exception. Saving Country Music (CW-S18) says nearly every song turns on a woman, a broken heart and drinking, and it praises the few tracks with a distinct angle, such as 'Jack and Jill' playing on nursery-rhyme language. Wallen himself (Morgan Wallen Radio, via Holler CW-S38) admits 37 songs risk monotony; his fix was sequencing ('two country, one cross'), which answers the problem with sound rather than with lyrics.
quote: more formulaic than totemic
why_it_matters: Across a body of work, vary the situation and the angle, not only the production, because critics notice when one emotional scenario keeps coming back.
when_not: These are critics' judgements of novelty, not of appeal; NPR (CW-S17) notes nearly all 37 tracks reached the Hot 100.

source: CW-S49#paras quoting Bryan; synthesis with CW-F1 to CW-F14
finding: My synthesis of what transfers and what belongs to the genre. Methods the writers describe without reference to country sound look like general craft: flipping an idiom (CW-F8), finding the detail that makes a title true for the singer (CW-F9), singing a title to test it (CW-F6), fitting words to a melody's sounds (CW-F7), and throwing out a 'B' song (CW-F12). Genre convention covers the drinking, truck and small-town vocabulary (CW-F11, CW-F14), spoken 'talking country' verses (CW-F10) and the blame-trading heartbreak persona (CW-F5); beat-first, artist-targeted quick writes (CW-F1, CW-F4) and long credit lists (CW-F13) are effects of the industry system rather than craft. By contrast, sole writer Zach Bryan says 'Something in the Orange' grew from thinking about the word 'orange' while watching a sunset alone in a cabin, not from a turned phrase, and Chartmetric (CW-S36) treats him as the outlier to the many-writer trend; search-result headlines suggest his account has varied in later interviews, but those pages were not fetched, so that is unverified.
why_it_matters: Borrow the Nashville room's methods (the flip, the revealing detail, the sing-test, the cull) without adopting its default vocabulary or persona.
when_not: The sorting is my own, and several of the 'general' techniques are documented here mainly from country writers, so how well they transfer to other genres is untested.

source: CT-S1#whole article: word stress, 4/4 strong beats, 'come back' vs 'bridegroom' mismatch
finding: Pattison's core rule is to set stressed syllables on stressed musical positions and unstressed syllables on weak ones; in 4/4 he treats beats 1 and 3 as strong and repeats that strong/weak pattern at the eighth-note level. Content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) normally carry stress, while articles, prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliaries and pronouns don't unless the line needs contrast. His bad-setting example puts a plea of 'come back' on a rhythm shaped like the word 'bridegroom', flipping the natural stress: stressed syllables on weak positions sound hurried, unstressed ones on strong beats sound flat. Keppie Coutts (CT-S2) adds that pronouns and endings like -ty and -ly are the syllables songs most often mis-stress.
quote: a song is simply natural speech, exaggerated.
why_it_matters: Speak the line at normal pace, mark the stresses, and check every stressed syllable lands where the melody leans; fix mismatches by changing word order or word choice before touching the tune.
when_not: Coutts (CT-S2) reports a student line that deliberately stressed the weak word 'for' and was kept after John Mayer judged the missetting itself expressive: breaks work when chosen, not when accidental.

source: CT-S3#sections on prosody, line length, rhyme scheme and space after key lines
finding: Pattison treats a section's shape as part of what it says: even line counts, matched line lengths, a steady number of stresses per line, and AABB or ABAB rhyme feel settled; an odd line count, one line clearly shorter or longer than the rest, shifting stress counts, and ABBA feel unsettled (same toolkit in CT-S4 and CT-S5). His warning example is a heartbreak verse in four equal AABB lines, which he says reads like reported facts rather than felt pain; his fixes include shortening the fourth line, lengthening the last, an asymmetric rhyme scheme, or displacing the melody against the chord cycle. He also says the most important line needs space after it, such as a turnaround, so it can land, and should not compete for room with lesser ideas.
quote: sounds like you're just telling me facts!
why_it_matters: If the words say 'unresolved' but the section is four tidy, equal, perfectly rhymed lines, change the shape (line count, last-line length, rhyme order) before rewriting the words.
when_not: He presents these as tools, not rules: settled feelings suit stable shapes, and most songs mix stable and unstable sections.

finding: Pattison ranks rhyme by how closed it sounds. Perfect rhyme (same stressed vowel and following consonants, different opening sound, e.g. fire/desire) resolves; family rhyme (same vowel, related consonants, e.g. mud/truck) nearly resolves; assonance (vowel only, e.g. read/cheap) stays open. He argues the more distant types can carry unresolved feeling that perfect rhyme can't, so choosing the rhyme type is part of prosody rather than a compromise.
why_it_matters: Use rhyme type as a dial: perfect rhyme where the thought lands or resolves, vowel-only rhyme where it should stay open or uneasy.
when_not: Nothing fetched for this slice states that slant rhyme is the modern default; Pattison frames it as a choice matched to feeling, not a norm.

source: CT-S39#Sloan on 'God's Plan' (rhyme and repetition passage)
finding: Musicologist Nate Sloan (Switched On Pop) says Drake's 'God's Plan' relies heavily on identity rhymes, rhyming a word with itself, and otherwise on near or slant rhymes, with a lot of repetition. In the same conversation he describes Post Malone's 'Circles' as returning to one melodic fragment again and again. This is an analyst describing finished records, not the writers' own account, and we have no audio to check it.
quote: Drake uses a lot of what are called identity rhymes.
why_it_matters: In current pop and rap, landing the same word again at the rhyme position is an accepted move, which takes pressure off forcing a perfect rhyme.
when_not: Our inference: identity rhyme leans on groove and delivery; in a sparse ballad the same move can read as lazy.

source: CT-S10#Kotecha's quoted remarks on melody as 'math' and the pre-chorus fix
finding: Savan Kotecha says that when a melodic phrase repeats, each repeat's lyric has to match it syllable for syllable; adding or dropping a single syllable breaks the pattern. His second concrete fix: if verse, pre-chorus and chorus all start ahead of the downbeat and the chorus doesn't lift, move the pre-chorus so it starts after beat one. Emily Warren (CT-S11) and Pat Pattison (CT-S3) both advise varying where phrases start against the downbeat, and Nate Sloan (CT-S40) describes the first vocal of 'Call Me Maybe' as waiting past beat one to create nervous suspense (his reading; no audio checked).
quote: you mess up the 'math'
why_it_matters: When a rewrite touches a line sung to a repeated melody, keep its syllable count identical to the matching line; when a chorus feels flat, try changing where the previous section starts before rewriting the chorus.
when_not: Julia Michaels (CT-S20) says she writes from feeling and doesn't think about a song's mathematics at all.

source: CT-S11#Warren's tips on chorus-first, story map, pre-chorus, range and rhythmic entry
finding: Emily Warren writes the chorus first, then maps the story the verses and pre-chorus tell on the way to it. She writes the pre-chorus lyric as a cliffhanger that leaves the listener needing the chorus, and puts each section in its own range, usually verse lowest, pre-chorus higher with tenser notes, chorus highest, while saying the contrast matters more than that order. Gary Ewer (CT-S12) adds that the pre-chorus chords should end pointing at the chorus's first chord and that the section is optional; Rami Yacoub (CT-S13) says a chorus that doesn't land may really be a pre-chorus failing to set it up.
quote: leaves you NEEDING the chorus, like a cliffhanger of sorts
why_it_matters: Write the pre-chorus as an open question or rising pressure that only the chorus answers; when a chorus feels weak, rewrite the pre-chorus first.
when_not: Ewer's test (CT-S12): after a few days away, sing straight from verse into chorus; if the chorus doesn't arrive too abruptly, a pre-chorus may be padding.

source: CT-S13#Yacoub on melodic math and the pre-chorus
finding: Rami Yacoub, a long-time member of Max Martin's team, says they don't start from melodic math: they write the melodies that come to them and reach for the rules when a section feels wrong (he speaks for his team; the article doesn't say Martin works this way). Martin (CT-S14) calls his theories useful when you get stuck and says feel comes first; Ryan Tedder (CT-S18) says there is a math to melody but he doesn't write with it, using it to get out of trouble. Asaf Peres (CT-S17), who sells a melodic-math course, says Martin hasn't used the term publicly and that it isn't a formula.
quote: We never start writing by implementing the melodic math
why_it_matters: Use syllable counts, range, entry points and section contrast as a checklist on a draft that isn't working, not as the generator of the first draft.

source: CT-S14#Martin on pairing busy and sparse sections, and on Prince's verse/chorus melody
finding: Max Martin says a section crowded with rhythm should be followed by one that isn't, with longer notes; using 'Shake It Off', he says that after a busy stretch the listener needs a few long notes to take it in, or it becomes too much information (also reported in CT-S15). He also describes singing the chorus melody in the verse, citing Prince's 'I Wanna Be Your Lover', so the chorus feels familiar the first time it arrives, with energy rather than melody changing. The quotes come from a Swedish interview (Di Weekend) and may be translated.
quote: Once the chorus comes, you feel like you've heard it before.
why_it_matters: After a dense, wordy line, give the next phrase fewer syllables and longer notes so the listener can catch up; at song speed, density has to be paid back.
when_not: Text only: whether 'Shake It Off' actually alternates this way is Martin's description, not something we checked by listening.

source: CT-S21#'Words + Music in 6 Seconds' sample quoted in the article
finding: Dan Wilson's short-form advice is to look after the sound of the words and their vowels first and trust that meaning will often follow. Max Martin (CT-S16, Telegraph interview via Variety) says much the same: he heard English lyrics as pure sound growing up, picks whichever word sounds most appealing, and says a line wins when it means something and has the right phonetics. Neither fetched source gives specific rules on which vowels suit held or high notes, consonant clusters, or elision, so that guidance is not sourced here.
quote: Take care of the sounds of the words and the vowels
why_it_matters: When two wordings mean the same thing, sing both on the actual note and keep the one that sounds better.
when_not: Finneas (CT-S31) calls himself a lyric person and finds boring lyrics on a beautiful melody less forgivable; Wilson himself calls lyrics the hardest part (CT-S23).

source: CT-S25#'John Cougar, John Deere, John 3:16' passage
song: John Cougar, John Deere, John 3:16 — Keith Urban
finding: Shane McAnally says one line of 'John Cougar, John Deere, John 3:16' came out of Ross Copperman singing wordless vowel sounds over the track: the writers found real words inside those syllables. Jack Antonoff (CT-S27) argues that singing a goofy placeholder lyric frees people to find a better melody, and Finneas (CT-S28) describes improvising placeholder lyrics into being on 'bad guy' before working out rhymes and story. In each case melody and sound come first, and the final words are fitted into a shape the placeholder syllables already set.
quote: It was just syllables.
why_it_matters: Our inference for the app: when a co-writer has a sung placeholder, treat its syllable count and stressed vowels as the template and propose real words that fit it, rather than reshaping the melody around new words.
when_not: Lori McKenna (CT-S34) mostly starts from the lyric and asks what it wants to sound like.

finding: Shane McAnally tells writers to put it in a song the way it happened and the way they'd say it in conversation; he distrusts a song that works too neatly, because that often means it wasn't written naturally, and advises keeping the true version and tweaking only what doesn't work. Julia Michaels (CT-S29) says writers often assume love songs need a grand metaphor when they can simply talk about love; a plain phrase she said mid-conversation became 'Love Is Weird' after co-writer Billy Walsh flagged it. Finneas (CT-S30) adds the singer-specific version: lyrics for Billie Eilish must feel completely authentic to her, so the test is whether this singer would say it.
quote: write the way it happened
why_it_matters: Read the line aloud as if speaking to the person it addresses; if neither you nor the singer would ever say it that way, rephrase toward how you would.
when_not: Plain doesn't mean only common words: Finneas (CT-S31) finds it satisfying to use words that aren't used every day.

source: CT-S32#Tranter on opening conversations and the Reneé Rapp songs
finding: Justin Tranter starts sessions with a friendly conversation that doubles as an interview, and when the artist says something that could be a title or topic, keeps exploring it. For Reneé Rapp's 'Gemini Moon' and 'Pretty Girls', he says he wrote down what she said about a relationship, put her exact phrases into the songs, and wrote more poetic lines around them.
quote: surround those quotes with poetry
why_it_matters: Capture the artist's exact spoken wording in the session and build lines around it instead of translating it into 'lyric language'.

source: CT-S33#Tranter on the different jobs of verse and chorus
finding: Tranter says the chorus should explain the whole song and be universal enough that everyone wants to sing it, while the verses, and sometimes the pre-chorus, uncover the specific details. Emily Warren (CT-S11) passes on a saying with the same split: the verses are for the writer and can be as poetic as they like, the chorus is for the audience and should be simple to sing along to.
quote: know what the whole song is about inside the chorus
why_it_matters: Test the chorus on its own: someone hearing only it should be able to say what the song is about; keep private specifics in the verses.
when_not: Switched On Pop's verse-episode description (CT-S43) argues the chorus payoff depends on the verse setup, so a universal chorus still needs specific verses.

finding: Lori McKenna prefers songs that describe the room in close detail but may not say what the people feel, leaving the listener to decide; one well-chosen detail can reveal more about a person or the song's emotion than naming it. She also values a verse that sets a poetic line beside a plain domestic one. Separately (CT-S35), Billie Eilish says she feared a line in 'What Was I Made For?' that doesn't explain itself would be missed, and it turned out to be the first lyric listeners understood.
quote: a detail that makes you understand so much more
why_it_matters: Swap a stated feeling for one concrete object or action that implies it, and trust the listener to make the connection.
when_not: Tranter's split (CT-F13) keeps the chorus plain and universal; implied detail is mainly a verse tool.

source: CT-S36#McKenna and Lindsey on the title and the first verse
finding: 'Girl Crush' began with a title McKenna had seen as a social-media tag, normally used for admiring another woman rather than romance; she says the song could have gone many ways, and Hillary Lindsey says it could have been an empowerment song and didn't have to be about jealousy. Lindsey says they never discussed the title before diving in and that the song took shape once the first four lines came out (CT-S37 puts the session at about 40 minutes; CT-S36 quotes McKenna saying an hour and a half). The concept (the phrase) was fixed; the angle was chosen in the writing. Our reading of Lindsey's remark is that the finished angle is jealousy, which turns the phrase against its usual sense.
quote: That song could have gone in many directions.
why_it_matters: A title phrase with an everyday meaning is a concept, not yet an angle; list the angles it allows and choose the one that turns the phrase.

source: CT-S19#Tedder on what makes a hook
finding: Ryan Tedder describes a hook as a simple melody carrying a basic human concept phrased in a way that hasn't been said before, and cites Toni Braxton's 'Un-Break My Heart' as an everyday feeling given new wording. He adds that the hook can be the track itself, that on 'Good Life' the real hook is the post-hook after the chorus, and that a riff becomes the hook once it moves from supporting the song to leading it.
quote: No one had ever said it like that.
why_it_matters: Keep the feeling ordinary and make the phrasing new: the angle usually lives in the title's wording, not in an unusual topic.
when_not: In the same interview he says current hits lean on rhythm, repetition and one phrase that captures the track, so a fresh phrase may also need to be short and repeatable.

source: CT-S38#opening sections of the post (before paywall)
finding: Writing about 'Last Friday Night (T.G.I.F.)', Bonnie McKee says the song was fast, very rhythmic and had little repetition, so every line had to be either a clear visual picture or a very conversational phrase that was easy to sing; with no repeated hook to lean on, the words carried the song. She describes starting from a long list of words and phrases that fit the mood and cutting tame lines in favour of more vivid ones.
quote: the lyrics had to do all the heavy lifting
why_it_matters: In a fast, wordy section the listener gets one pass at each line, so each should be an instant picture or a phrase people already say.
when_not: Partial access: the post is paywalled after the opening, and her draft pages were not read.

finding: Switched On Pop's description of its bridge episode frames the bridge as a fresh-air contrast placed just before the final chorus that, at its best, changes the song's meaning by bringing in doubt or defiance; it notes critics fear the bridge is disappearing and asks why an artist might skip it. The guest, Tayla Parx, could not be read: no transcript was available and the show's own episode page failed to load (CT-S82). Ewer (CT-S12) calls the bridge optional, and Tedder (CT-S18) cites a hit built only of verses and choruses.
why_it_matters: Keep a bridge when it brings a new stance (doubt, defiance, reversal); if it only restates the chorus feeling over new chords, consider cutting it.
when_not: This is the show's framing, not a writer's documented reasoning; treat as provisional.

finding: Co-writer Steph Jones (told to Variety, relayed by ABC Audio) says the chorus started when Carpenter hummed a melody and the room asked what it was. He says they doubted the line that became the signature hook would survive because it seemed silly, and kept it anyway. He also traces a verse line (the 'working late 'cause I'm a singer' excuse) to the session itself: a studio outside Paris with beds upstairs so the team could work very late.
quote: Will this line stay? It's kind of silly
why_it_matters: If the room calls a line silly but it sits on the melody, test it as the hook before you cut it. A literal fact about the writing day can also become a self-mocking line.
when_not: This is a second-hand relay and says nothing about the silly lines that were dropped.

finding: Julian Bunetta says there was no concept going in. Carpenter wanted something fun and started from the tempo, he built a loop and bassline, and Carpenter, Amy Allen and Steph Jones traded sung parts over it. In a burst of about 20 minutes the words came out and the title arrived. They then spent three or four more hours refining, including changing some words. Ad libs Carpenter sang in the first session were later stitched into deliberate melodies.
quote: the words were just coming out and suddenly we had 'Espresso'
why_it_matters: A title can come out of sung improvisation over a groove. The long pass afterwards is for word-level edits, not for starting again.
when_not: Bunetta does not say which words changed, so there is no documented before and after.

source: PA-S1#midpoint, start of second half (after Hirway asks whether a vocal note change was planned)
finding: On Song Exploder, Carpenter explains how a vocal phrasing was chosen on 'Please Please Please'. That song is assigned to another agent; it is used here only for her general method. She says much of it was first instinct and how she would actually say the words in real life, and that her favourite thing in a song is to act, picturing the conversation with the person while she sings. Earlier (second quarter), Antonoff says many lyrics were literal things she had said in conversation. A year later, talking to Zane Lowe about Man's Best Friend (PA-S14, under the heading about being more theatrical), she says the storytelling and performance depend on how she sings a line, and that she weighed what would be most theatrical to sing while writing.
quote: the way that I would really say those things
why_it_matters: Say the line aloud as the narrator, to the person. When two lines are equally true, choose the one that gives the singer an attitude to perform.
when_not: This suits conversational, character-led pop. A line chosen for theatre can look gauche on the page (PA-F15), and this is text-only evidence with no audio heard.

finding: Carpenter describes the spoken 'Oh, boy' that opens 'Manchild', and the album, as a breath and an eye roll before going back into the story. Talking to Zane Lowe (PA-S14, 'On the story behind Man's Best Friend') she calls the opener an eye roll at herself, a here-we-go-again. Her Instagram announcement (PA-S13, para 7) frames it as an affectionate eye roll. So the opening gesture sets a weary, fond, partly self-directed stance before any insult arrives.
quote: a deep breath and an eye roll
why_it_matters: A spoken interjection at the top can set the narrator's attitude, so the complaints that follow land as fond exasperation rather than bitterness.
when_not: The effect depends on delivery. On paper the interjection carries almost nothing.

finding: Ailsa Chang asked whether the Carpenter team ever wrote something that felt too far. Amy Allen says it happened many times. She describes a small internal flag (too weird, too pop, pushing it too far) and says the flagged moment is usually the best part, the part listeners love about nine times in ten, so she chases it. Her example is a profane line in an earlier Carpenter single that the room laughed at and that became a much-loved moment. Carpenter gives the same picture in the Apple Music note (PA-S6): much of Short n' Sweet came from moments she couldn't stop laughing about, and a recurring joke could become a whole song. In Rolling Stone (PA-S5, para 5) she says her near-idiotic, funniest lines only happen with collaborators she is comfortable with.
quote: It's usually the best part of the song.
why_it_matters: Treat a co-writer's flinch, or a joke the room keeps coming back to, as a reason to keep and test the line, not as an automatic cut.
when_not: By her own count about one flagged moment in ten doesn't work. Critics found the joke density wearing by the 2025 album (PA-F15).

finding: Dan Nigro says the song was first titled 'Good Luck, Jane!'. After back-and-forth they switched to 'Babe' because it felt more sarcastic and playful. In Billboard (PA-S20, answer 1) he says Roan had been set on a proper name. In a Konbini quote relayed by NBC Insider (PA-S23), Roan says she and her co-writer kept arguing about it until it became 'Babe'. The edit is one word, the address term inside the title.
quote: just felt more sarcastic and playful
why_it_matters: The address word in a title can set the song's tone. An endearment can carry a sarcasm that a specific name cannot.
when_not: A name gives specificity and story. Nigro presents this as a tone choice, not a rule against names.

finding: Asked how the verses changed from the first draft, Nigro says the early lyrics were sharper and more barbed. They wanted the words to feel more effortless, casual and laid-back. He recalls Roan saying from the couch that she wanted a line about her arms reaching out of a sunroof, which he found funny and presents as a lighter moment in the verse.
why_it_matters: If a hurt song feels strained, try lowering the verbal temperature of the verses and adding one carefree physical image. The chorus can keep the force.
when_not: The original lines are not documented, so only the direction of the edit is known.

finding: Nigro says that when they reopened the song they narrowed in on the chorus and decided some of its words had to be sung in full voice. Listening back, they felt that solved it. In Music Week (PA-S19) he adds that on another pass he realised the song was in the wrong key. The chorus fix he describes is about register and key, not new words.
quote: some of the words needed to be in full voice
why_it_matters: A chorus that isn't landing may need a change of register on chosen words, or a key change, rather than a rewrite.
when_not: He doesn't say which words, or what register they replaced. With no audio, this stays provisional.

finding: Nigro says Roan wrote the bridge alone in about two minutes. She asked him to loop the pre-chorus chords and sang over them while he urged her to go further. In Music Week (PA-S19, para 8) he says the hard part of writing is the vocals, lyrics and emotion, and once those were nailed things like the bridge came easily. A Vulture critic later singled out the bridge's storytelling (reported in PA-S21).
why_it_matters: Once the chorus's emotional claim is settled, a bridge can be improvised quickly over borrowed pre-chorus harmony, pushed further than feels comfortable.
when_not: It was quick only because the song had been worked on for about a year. That is not evidence that bridges should be fast.

finding: Roan says 'The Subway' is about failing to get over one person: the feelings are still there although it is over. She says it took an irritatingly long time to get right. Talking about the video, she calls it serious and not serious at once, and cites the lyric about moving to Saskatchewan to show it isn't that serious. Consequence's critic (PA-S26, paras 3 and 6) praises a line he reads as a playful threat to move away, apparently the same line, and says the writing has more subtlety and distance than Roan usually goes for.
quote: a serious song, but at the same time it's not
why_it_matters: One absurdly specific escape plan inside a grief song lets the narrator admit the hurt without self-pity.
when_not: Her remark is framed around the video. She doesn't say the line was written as comic relief.

song: Birds of a Feather — Billie Eilish
finding: Songfacts relays a YouTube video, so this is second-hand. In it Finneas says there are many songs about dying for someone or loving them until death, and that he found it fun to reverse that; the source doesn't spell out what the reversed version is. Eilish says she wanted the song to feel a little toxic and love-bomb-y. In the WSJ interview relayed by Rolling Stone (PA-S30, para 5), she says they slipped in something dark, the idea that you will die soon so make it last, so the song wasn't all sweetness.
quote: I thought it was really fun to reverse it
why_it_matters: Name the stock trope your idea sits next to and deliberately turn it. A thread of darkness keeps a bright devotion song from being only bright.
when_not: The source doesn't say what was reversed, so don't over-read the mechanism.

song: Birds of a Feather — Billie Eilish
finding: Per Eilish's WSJ interview, relayed by Rolling Stone, she wanted to cut the song several times and told the label it was a bit stupid when she played them the album. The report says she and Finneas struggled to land the chorus, especially the delivery of its till-death vow line. Billboard (PA-S31) reports the song became Spotify's most-streamed song of 2024 and spent three weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Global 200; the chart weeks were not checked here.
quote: Guys, this one is kind of stupid.
why_it_matters: A writer's embarrassment at a simple, sincere chorus is not a reliable signal of its worth.
when_not: One hit doesn't mean every song a writer doubts should be kept. The report doesn't say whether the trouble was in the words or the singing.

finding: In the Apple Music track notes, Eilish says one verse came after a conversation with a friend. She decided to pretend to be that friend and write, and to put jokes in. She contrasts this with Happier Than Ever, which she says took itself too seriously, and says embracing cringe made her happier. On NPR Morning Edition (PA-S34, para 28) she says they had only the hook at first and came back about a year later to write the rest. She calls the song fun and silly.
quote: When you start to embrace cringe, you're so much happier.
why_it_matters: Writing a verse in a friend's voice, with jokes allowed, can free a desire song from solemnity. A strong hook can wait a year for its verses.
when_not: She frames this as a correction to her own previous album. It's no help to a writer who already leans comic.

finding: In the Apple Music track notes, Eilish calls 'Wildflower' a girl-code song about breaking girl code. She says it is not about cheating. She puts the problem not in any doubt about the partner's love, which the narrator accepts, but in a feeling the narrator can't shake. The conflict sits inside the narrator and her loyalty to a friend, not in the couple.
why_it_matters: Granting the partner's love up front moves the drama inside the narrator, so the song reads as a confession rather than a complaint.
when_not: Eilish never named specifics. Readings that identify real people are press speculation (PA-S37).

finding: Slant's Sal Cinquemani says Man's Best Friend leans too heavily on expletives, puns and cheeky one-liners, and that her effortless delivery makes the leaning more obvious. He finds the volume of sexual wordplay dulling and says no rhymes are subverted. He still reads 'Tears' as partly taking the piss. Wikipedia (PA-S16, PA-S17) reports similar complaints, not fetched here: the LA Times said 'Tears' reached for a memeable lyric, the Independent said the album felt like a first draft, and the Guardian flagged an internet-worn line.
quote: the sheer volume of her libidinous linguistics can be dulling
why_it_matters: A pun-and-innuendo voice needs rationing. When every line winks, none lands as a reveal.
when_not: This is criticism, not evidence of intent. NME and the London Standard praised the same double entendre on 'Tears' (PA-S17).

source: PA-S14#'On the story behind Man's Best Friend'
finding: My inference, across PA-F4 (Manchild: an eye roll partly at herself), PA-F10 (The Subway: serious and not), PA-F14 (Wildflower: the problem is the narrator's own feeling) and PA-F13 (Lunch: embrace cringe). In this slice, hurt or desire is often carried by a narrator who implicates or mocks herself before she accuses anyone, and the writers describe that tone as deliberate. The exception is 'Good Luck, Babe!', where Roan describes writing from anger (PA-S22, para 11) and the sarcasm points outward through the title.
why_it_matters: If the narrator rolls her eyes at herself first, the listener will let her be harsh about the other person.
when_not: 'Good Luck, Babe!' points outward and works, so self-mockery is one route, not a rule.

source: PB-S1#early-middle, answer to how writing with Hobert differs from ordinary conversation
song: I Love You, I'm Sorry — Gracie Abrams
finding: Abrams says writing with Audrey Hobert, a close friend, strips out the politeness of a normal session: nobody's feelings get hurt, so lines are offered and thrown out fast. Of the candidate lines, they often keep the one that makes them laugh most, and she describes the laughing as how the two of them got through big, uncomfortable adult feelings. In the voice memos, Hobert's approving 'ooh' marks a line as funny enough to keep.
quote: going with the line that makes us laugh the hardest
why_it_matters: Use laughter in the room as the test for a blunt or hurt line: if it makes the writers laugh, it usually carries the wound and the self-awareness together.
when_not: Abrams also says some lines that got a laugh sound weak on playback, and Hobert says she is not a writer who can work with just anyone (PB-S11 P9), so the test needs trust between the writers and a cold re-listen afterwards.

source: PB-S1#middle to late-middle: verse breakdown with Dessner's production; bridge discussion
song: I Love You, I'm Sorry — Gracie Abrams
finding: Abrams says she built the song in chapters across time rather than one moment. Verse one recalls an honest confession that went badly and the other person leaving. Verse two is what she calls the petty part: she watches the ex charm people at events on his own and judges him from a distance. A later section pictures them friendly years later. Most of the album's bridges rush along as manic thought, she says, but here she wanted a rhythmic change, and the bridge is where she owns her behaviour as a habit to break. She also admits a verse line hurt its subject and that she has been careless before about how people take songs written about them.
why_it_matters: Let the verses hold the past and the pettiness, and keep the bridge for the narrator's own admission, set apart by a change of rhythm rather than more speed.
when_not: Abrams' regret about hurting the subject is the cost: a petty verse works on record, but the person it is about will hear it.

source: PB-S1#late, answer to Hirway's question about the title format
song: I Love You, I'm Sorry — Gracie Abrams
finding: Abrams says the title's shape comes from an earlier song of hers, I Miss You, I'm Sorry, about the same person, and from years of drafts that used a hate version of the same formula. The formula stuck with her as a fixed point she kept coming back to. She says the feeling in the new pairing is sincere. Wikipedia also relays her telling Today (2024-07-18) that the song is a bookend to the earlier one (PB-S2).
why_it_matters: Reusing one title template across songs to the same person turns two flat clauses into an ongoing conversation, and changing the single verb shows how the relationship has moved.
when_not: The template depends on the earlier song being known; heard on its own, the title is simply two stock phrases side by side.

finding: On Song Exploder, Abrams says her voice memos come out half-mumbled, somewhere between speaking and singing, and calls this a mouth-feel thing: words are kept for how they sit in the mouth as well as for what they mean (PB-S1). In Nylon, Hobert says Abrams taught her the idea of mouthfeel, meaning checking whether words feel good strung together, and that it stayed with her. Hobert was explaining why Abrams' songs stick even when they make odd choices. She was not talking about That's So True in particular.
quote: when you see if words feel good all strung together
why_it_matters: Mumble a line before fixing its words, and judge plain conversational phrases by how they feel said one after another, not only by their sense.
when_not: Neither source gives an example of a word changed for mouthfeel, so the practice is stated rather than shown. Any judgement about how the words sound is provisional, since I worked from text only.

finding: Abrams told Nylon (Dec 2024) that she and Hobert were drunk on the roof of Electric Lady Studios when they wrote the lyric, laughing to the point of tears. She called it an angsty, sarcastic song and said the first lyrics were much nastier. Second-hand reports of a Spotify event (PB-S6, PB-S7) have her saying a far cruder version exists that will never come out. Nylon's writer, not Abrams, reads the bridge as a rushed, panicked confession. In October 2025 Abrams told People she was nervous about discussing the bridge and would not take it apart (PB-S5).
why_it_matters: Draft the jealous, unreasonable version at full ugliness for the laugh, then file it down to sarcasm: the attitude survives without the vulgarity. My inference, not Abrams' statement: a stock agreeing reply such as That's So True works as a sarcastic title once the song around it is angsty.
when_not: The evidence is thin and partly second-hand, and no source says which lines changed between the crude draft and the release.

finding: Hobert says that what she disliked in school poetry was flowery language, and that her rule for herself is to say plainly what she wants to say. She names her two goals as making people laugh and telling the truth. Her favourite line in Sue Me hangs on a real, petty detail: the clothing brand an ex always wore. W Magazine reports that the Sue Me chorus came out while she was venting to producer Ricky Gourmet and that she sang it straight away. The same piece says, in the writer's words, that she drafts lyrics like monologues and edits them for clarity and rhythm (PB-S10).
quote: My goals are to make them laugh and tell the truth
why_it_matters: A small, checkable, petty detail such as a brand or an object makes a grudge funny and believable at once, and stating it plainly beats decorating it.
when_not: Paste's critic (PB-S14, entry #11) heard Sue Me as affected diary-pop whose chorus works by brute repetition. The plain, quirky approach reads as a pose when the detail feels styled rather than lived.
